items.title: Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
items.summary: This post announces native PyTorch backends for vLLM and SGLang powered by TorchTPU, enabling developers to run and optimize serving workloads using familiar PyTorch tools. Built in collaboration with open-source project maintainers, these engines include optimized TPU kernel implementations, production-ready features like KV cache management with TPU Sync, and disaggregated serving. Public benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and industry-leading cost efficiency on Ironwood TPU across long-context and agentic workloads.

items.title: Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
items.summary: Google Workspace now offers native support for Markdown (.md) files, allowing developers and AI agents to seamlessly collaborate on documentation directly in Google Docs without manual file conversions. This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.

items.title: Building Conversational Commerce with Multi-Agent Swarms on GCP: A Working Prototype
items.summary: This document provides a publication template and metadata structure for a technical blog post focused on building Conversational User Interfaces (CUIs) using AI. It outlines key developer focus areas, product stacks, and approval workflows required for publishing technical content through Google Developer Studio. The framework helps engineers organize their guides and solutions to effectively share AI-driven conversational interface designs with the developer community.

items.title: Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents
items.summary: See Google A2Ui in action! Learn how to natively render agentic UIs across Langchain, AWS Strands, Microsoft agents, and Google ADK using CopilotKit SDKs for A2UI.

items.title: Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond
items.summary: The Agents CLI Extension System enables developers to use frameworks like LangChain, LangGraph, or custom enterprise stacks while retaining a unified deployment and evaluation workflow. It details a first-party LangChain template that scaffolds, runs, and deploys agents without requiring the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Additionally, it demonstrates how platform teams can author custom extensions to enforce policies such as automated software bill of materials (SBOM) scans during deployment.

items.title: DevFest is back!
items.summary: DevFest 2026 runs from October 1 to December 31, bringing together nearly a million developers across more than 800 global events centered on the agentic AI era. Under the theme "Build, Secure, Scale," participants gain hands-on experience with Google’s developer stack—including Gemini, Google AI Studio, Google Antigravity, and Web MCP—through live workshops and codelabs. The conference focuses on enabling developers to prototype rapidly, ensure secure and private deployments, and leverage production-ready infrastructure.

items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
items.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

items.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
items.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. These updates require no changes to frontend renderers or component catalogs, offering flexible performance levers for generative UI development across Python, TypeScript, and Dart.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
items.summary: Google Research has completed the 32-bit open-source Coral NPU RISC-V architecture with the introduction of its Matrix Execution Unit, which delivers up to 1 TOPS while targeting 10 mW average power for edge inference. Alongside this architecture, the release of the v1.0 open-source IREE/MLIR compiler allows developers to take models from JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow straight to Coral NPU hardware without writing custom assembly. Developers can now prototype and deploy these multimodal edge applications using new hardware options like the Synaptics Astra SR200 MCU series and globally available Coralboard devkits.12

items.title: Step by Step guide: Build a Voice Agent That Never Goes Silent using ADK
items.summary: The open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK) and gemini-3.8-live enable developers to build responsive voice agents by implementing non-blocking tools in Python. Developers can use streaming tools to yield progress updates or background execution patterns to keep conversations fluid during long-running backend queries. Additionally, configuring response scheduling behaviors such as WHEN_IDLE, INTERRUPT, or SILENT gives developers precise control over when and how tool results are delivered into the conversation.

items.title: Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer
items.summary: Google AI Edge Model Explorer now supports custom compiler intermediate representations and open-source adapters like TOSA, VGF, and PTE for on-device machine learning. Developers can leverage hierarchical graph visualization, split-pane views, and per-node trace overlays to catch export regressions and verify hardware delegation. These tools enable engineering teams to transparently debug execution graphs and pinpoint cycle-level latency bottlenecks locally.

items.title: Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec
items.summary: API Gateway now supports real-time streaming—including Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, gRPC, and chunked transfer encoding—in Public Preview without requiring changes to your existing API specifications. This update allows developers to route long-lived, bi-directional streams and AI workloads directly through the gateway while maintaining consistent authentication, rate limiting, and observability. Additionally, gateways now feature deterministic default hostnames, simplifying environment provisioning and infrastructure-as-code management.

items.title: Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services
items.summary: LiteRT in Google Play services now offers GPU inference powered by ML Drift, delivering about 1.4x faster performance alongside the new CompiledModel API. Switching from bundled binaries reduces app size by approximately 8 MB while enabling seamless, automatic runtime updates across billions of devices. Developers can easily adopt these updates by updating their dependencies and utilizing the new Android Studio LiteRT skill for automated migration.

items.title: Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud
items.summary: Learn how Project Chrysalis combines Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Agent Development Kit (ADK), BigQuery, and a four-gate defense-in-depth security stack (Model Armor, Cloud KMS, Binary Authorization, and OPA) to build governed, self-evolving AI agents that remediate live production outages in 1.8 seconds.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation
items.summary: This post walks through the Agents CLI evaluation loop for systematically improving agent performance through continuous testing and grading. It demonstrates how to catch prompt regressions, evaluate model backend swaps using side-by-side trace comparisons, and automate evaluation passes. Developers will also learn how to integrate nightly scheduled runs with threshold-based alerting to track quality over time.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: From prompt to app: Build with Google Maps in AI Studio
items.summary: Developers can now build applications powered by Google Maps Platform directly within Google AI Studio by prompting Gemini with real-world geospatial concepts. The integration eliminates traditional configuration hurdles by providing one-click demo keys that generate instantly without requiring Cloud Console redirects or credit cards. This setup grants developers immediate access to core APIs—including Maps, Places, and Routes—supported by daily sandbox quotas for seamless prototyping.

Here is how to handle RAR archives in 2026 without surprises. Both use the .rar extension, and they are incompatible on disk. items.title: Why Your Server Keeps Crashing: Understanding Memory Leaks in Node.js
items.summary: A memory leak occurs when a computer program incorrectly manages memory allocations, failing to release memory that is no longer needed. Essentially, your application asks for RAM from the system but forgets to give it back, eventually causing the system to run out of available memory. Imagine you are checking books out of a library, but instead of returning them, you keep them in your backpack forever. At first, your backpack is light. By the tenth book, it’s heavy. Eventually, you have no more space to store anything else, and you are forced to stop visiting the library entirely. In software, your code is the library patron, and the RAM is the backpack space; if you never release your references to objects, the system can't reuse that space. In the real world, developers use memory management tools to keep services stable. Without these checks, an application might start perfectly fine but degrade over time, leading to "Out of Memory" (OOM) crashes in production. For a MERN developer, this usually means an Express.js API slowing down until it hangs, requiring a manual restart of the Node.js process. items.title: API business logic abuse: requests that are valid but wrong
items.summary: API business logic abuse: requests that are valid but wrong Akamai's Apps, APIs, and DDoS 2026 report counted an average of 258 API attacks per enterprise in 2025, up 113% from 121 in 2024. The same report found that 61% of API attacks in 2025 involved unauthorized workflows and abnormal activity, up from 30% in 2024. Akamai's data comes from enterprise traffic. The pattern scales down without trouble. A five-person SaaS with a signup flow, a checkout and a search endpoint has the same exposure, and usually less logging to catch it with. Business logic abuse uses your API as built, in an order or at a volume you didn't plan for. Every request carries a valid token. Every body passes validation. The response is a 200. That leaves most of the usual tools with nothing to look at. A firewall injection rule matches payloads like ' OR 1=1, and there aren't any. Your error tracker records exceptions, and nothing threw. Uptime checks pass. The problem only shows up in the rate and order of requests per user, which most apps don't record. items.title: React's browser() API: Opt Out of SSR Without the Mounted-State Hack
items.summary: Every server-rendered React app eventually grows a component that just can't render on the server. It reads a draft from localStorage, shows the visitor's time zone, or wraps a charting library that touches window on import. So you reach for the usual workaround: a mounted flag set in an effect, or a typeof window !== 'undefined' check sprinkled through render. Both work, sort of. The effect version renders nothing (or a placeholder) on the first client pass and then flips, which costs you an extra render and some layout shift. The typeof window version is worse, because it renders different output on the server and the client, which is exactly how you get a hydration mismatch. React 19.3, released in September 2026, finally ships a real answer: use(browser()). browser() actually does browser is a new export from react-dom. items.title: Handling HEIC uploads from iPhones in 2026: what breaks and how to fix it
items.summary: A photo that looks fine on an iPhone can still fail the moment it hits your upload form. The preview is blank, the server rejects the file, or a thumbnail throws, and the report is usually "it is just a photo." It is often a HEIC file: the default iPhone still-image format, and still something most browsers will not display. I built heic.now because I kept hitting that failure in CMS uploads and client hand-offs, and I am the site's maker, so I will be explicit about that. Here is what actually breaks in 2026, and how to handle it. Since iOS 11, iPhones set to High Efficiency (Settings → Camera → Formats) write stills as HEIC: a HEIF container with HEVC-compressed image data. The files are smaller than a comparable JPEG, which is why Apple made them the default. They are not a JPEG with an unusual extension. Uploads from the iPhone itself often succeed anyway. When someone picks a photo from the iOS Photo Library in a web , iOS commonly transcodes it to JPEG before your page sees it — in Safari, Chrome, Firefox, and Edge on iOS, even if accept lists image/heic. items.title: Node.js 26's Map.getOrInsertComputed is slower than the get-and-set it replaces
items.summary: Node 26 shipped V8 14.6, and with it two new methods that have been asked for for years: Map.prototype.getOrInsert() and Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed(). Both are meant to replace the same five-line idiom everyone has copy-pasted into a cache or a memo table at some point: look up a key, and if it isn't there, compute a default, store it, and return it. I expected the built-in version to be at least as fast as the hand-written one, since it collapses two separate Map operations into one. It is not. On a warm cache it is about 40% slower than the code it replaces. That was the first surprise. The second is more useful: the same method quietly gives you cache-stampede protection for async work, for free, with no extra code. The third is that if the computation fails, it keeps the failure cached forever, with no obvious way to know that from the method's name alone. getOrInsertComputed(key, callbackfn) checks whether key is present. If it is, it returns the existing value and never touches callbackfn. items.title: turbopackRustReactCompiler: Running the React Compiler in Rust Inside Next.js
items.summary: This blog's next.config.mjs has two lines that look like they do the same thing: reactCompiler: true, experimental: { turbopackRustReactCompiler: true }, They don't. The first turns the React Compiler on. The second picks which version of it runs. Turbopack speaks Rust. The normal React Compiler speaks JavaScript. Without the flag, every component file goes through an interpreter: it's handed to Node.js, compiled there, and handed back. turbopackRustReactCompiler hires a native speaker instead: a Rust version of the compiler that runs inside Turbopack itself. Same work, same output. Just no interpreter in the middle. The React Compiler is a build step that adds memoization to your components for you. Memoization means "remember the last result and reuse it if the inputs didn't change". It's what useMemo, useCallback and memo do by hand (quick refresher here). // You write this: function Price({ amount }) { const label = formatMoney(amount); return {label} ; } // The compiler outputs a version that skips formatMoney // and reuses the same when amount hasn't changed. items.title: Your API Does Not Need More Logs. It Needs One Error Shape.
items.summary: Your API does not need more logs. It needs one error shape. A client I worked with kept breaking every time an endpoint failed. One error came back as plain text, the next as an HTML page, the next as a JSON object with a different field name each time. The frontend could not tell a missing order from a server crash, so it showed the same vague message for both. The frontend team had a different check for every endpoint, and every new endpoint added another guess. Support tickets said the same thing each time: "something went wrong." Nobody could say what, because the API never said what in a shape the client could read. The wrong fix is to write a better message for each endpoint. Better messages in five different shapes are still five different shapes. A clear message inside a shape the client cannot parse is still unreadable to the client. Every new endpoint adds one more shape for the client to guess, and the frontend grows a new special case for each one. Every error returns the same shape. items.title: One app, three native UIs: what I learned building the same app in SwiftUI, WinUI 3 and GTK 4
items.summary: I started this app as "GitHub Lite". All I wanted was a quick way to check my pull requests for new comments, because opening GitHub in the browser made my PC lag so badly that I couldn't work properly. Once that worked, I thought it would be better to automate the next step too, so I built "Fix with agent": it looks at the review comments (it doesn't fix anything itself), writes a prompt from them and starts an agent session to fix them. Then I realized I could do the whole loop inside the app: open the PR, review it, fix, re-request review, answer or leave comments, and so on. Today that app is called PullYard, and it exists three times: a Swift/SwiftUI app for macOS, a C#/WinUI 3 app for Windows, and a Rust/GTK 4 app for Linux. They share no code. Getting the Windows and Linux versions to launch took one day, but that was only launching and minimal functionality. After that I had to work seriously on security and memory leaks, and fix a lot of things. People who hear this tend to ask "why not Electron / Tauri / Flutter?" before anything else. items.title: How SSR Works in React and Next.js: Built on the Server, Wired Up in the Browser
items.summary: Open a Next.js page on a slow phone. The page shows up almost at once: text, images, a "Like" button. You tap the button and nothing happens. A second later you tap again and it works. Nothing was broken. You tapped during the gap between the two halves of server-side rendering. SSR delivers a fully built house with the electricity off. Hydration is the electrician walking through and connecting every switch to the wiring that's already there. The server builds the page as HTML, so you see it right away. But HTML can't run code, so nothing responds yet. Then the JavaScript arrives, and React connects your event handlers to the HTML that's already on screen. Only then does the house have power. One SSR request, from URL to working page 1. Request — The browser asks for /post/42 2. Server runs components — React calls your components on the server, with real data 3. HTML sent — A finished HTML page goes over the network 4. Browser paints — The user sees the page. Buttons don't work yet. 5. JS downloads — The browser fetches the JavaScript bundle for the page 6. Hydration — React runs the same components in the browser and compares ├─ Output matches the HTML → Attach event handlers →

items.title: How Next.js Turns JSX and TypeScript Into Plain JavaScript
items.summary: Paste one line of JSX into a browser console: const el = Hi ; // SyntaxError: Unexpected token ' means inside JavaScript. Neither does it understand : string or type Props. Yet every Next.js app is written in exactly that. Something sits between your editor and the browser, translating. The browser only speaks plain JavaScript. A compiler erases your types and rewrites every JSX tag as a function call, so what reaches the browser is ordinary JS. Types and JSX are for you and your editor. They never ship. Picture a translator who reads your file, crosses out the notes in the margins (types), and rewrites the shorthand (JSX) in full sentences (function calls). Here's a tiny TypeScript component: type Props = { name: string }; export function Hello({ name }: Props) { return Hi {name} ; } I ran it through SWC, the compiler bundled with Next.js 16.4, using the same JSX settings Next.js uses. This is the real output: import { jsxs as _jsxs } from "react/jsx-runtime"; export function Hello({ name }) { return /*#__PURE__*/ _jsxs("h1", { className: "title", children: ["Hi ", name], }); } Two things happened: Types were erased. type Props and : Props are gone. items.title: Aligning Internal Package Versions with .NET 10 Under SemVer: Principles and Team Communication
items.summary: The SemVer Specification Reality: What the Rules Actually Allow If you trace the literal text of the Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 specification, there is no mathematical restriction stopping you from jumping an internal package version from 2.0.0 to 10.0.0. The specification mandates that the MAJOR version increment when incompatible changes are introduced to the public API, but it is completely silent on step sizes, gaps, or sequential continuity. A dependency parser reading a version string evaluates numeric segments discretely, meaning 10.0.0 is syntactically valid immediately following 2.0.0. However, treating the SemVer specification solely as a syntax validator ignores the physical and mechanical reality of how version numbers function as information-theoretic signals within a software ecosystem. Version numbers operate as lossy compression channels meant to transmit risk, complexity, and API stability state to dependent systems and human consumers. items.summary: I maintain Blazor Blueprint, an open-source Blazor component library. I want to talk about something that shows up as soon as a schedule crosses a daylight-saving change, or has to work in more than one time zone: time. My day job is running a business that builds HRMS software. It's a regional application, and our customers have employees spread across different time zones. Shifts, leave, rosters, public holidays: scheduling sits right in the middle of it, so an accurate calendar matters a lot to me. When clocks spring forward, a night shift is an hour shorter. When they fall back, it is an hour longer. Get the local times wrong and you pay the wrong hours, or a start time lands in an hour that never happens. items.summary: I turned on output caching for a report endpoint that was getting hammered, patted myself on the back, and went to lunch. When I came back the server was still doing the exact same amount of work. Same CPU, same database chatter, same everything. The cache was on. I could see it in the config. It just wasn't catching anything. The endpoint was dead simple — a paginated report, /report?page=1, the kind of thing that's identical for every visitor on the same page. Perfect candidate for caching. So why was the handler running on basically every request? items.title: SecureStorageKit: a dependency-free Swift package for Keychain, Face ID and Secure Enclave storage
items.summary: Every iOS app I've worked on in the last decade ended up with its own hand-rolled Keychain wrapper. Most of them had the same bugs: errSecDuplicateItem not handled, queries that didn't match the attributes used to save, background reads failing with errSecInteractionNotAllowed and logging the user out, and tokens quietly ending up in print statements. So I packaged the patterns I keep rewriting into SecureStorageKit: a free, open-source Swift package for storing secrets on iOS, iPadOS and macOS. It's serverless, built only on Apple frameworks (Keychain, LocalAuthentication, CryptoKit and the Secure Enclave), and has no third-party dependencies. items.title: iOS Application Security: SSL Pinning, Keychain, API Encryption and App Attest
items.summary: iOS has a strong security baseline: code signing, sandboxing, App Transport Security, Data Protection and the Secure Enclave are all on by default. That baseline leads many teams to assume the platform covers everything. It doesn't. The platform protects the user from malicious apps very well, but it does much less to protect your backend from a modified copy of your app, a scripted client that impersonates it, or a user who deliberately intercepts their own traffic. This guide looks at four questions that come up in almost every security review of an iOS app. For each one, the goal is an honest answer: what the technique actually protects against, what it does not, and how to implement it correctly if you decide you need it. items.title: I Allocated 65 MB of Strings to Read Three Numbers
items.summary: I had a parser for a fixed-width settlement feed. Each line is 28 characters, no delimiters: an id, an amount, a quantity, all at known offsets. I needed three typed values out of every line and nothing else. So I wrote the obvious thing with Substring, it worked, and I moved on. Weeks later I was reading an allocation profile for an unrelated leak and this loop was sitting near the top, quietly handing the garbage collector 65 MB of strings I never kept. Here's the loop, cleaned up: foreach (var line in feed) { idSum += int.Parse(line.Substring(0, 10)); amtSum += decimal.Parse(line.Substring(10, 12), inv); qtySum += int.Parse(line.Substring(22, 6)); } Looks harmless. But Substring doesn't hand you a view into the original string, it cuts a brand-new one. Three calls per line means three fresh strings per record, each one alive just long enough to be parsed and then dropped. Over 500,000 lines that's 1.5 million little allocations, and the only thing I wanted out of the whole exercise was three running totals. I measured it with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around the loop rather than a timer. Allocation counts are deterministic, so the number doesn't wobble between runs

items.title: Building an iOS app blocker with the Screen Time API (FamilyControls) in Expo: what the docs don't tell you
items.summary: I spent the last few months building Prayer Lock, an iPhone app that blocks distracting apps during a scheduled daily prayer time. The whole product rests on Apple's Screen Time API: FamilyControls, ManagedSettings and DeviceActivity. The documentation is thin and the sharp edges are real. This is the write-up I wish I had on day one. The app is React Native (Expo) with a native Swift module, but almost everything below applies to a pure Swift app too. FamilyControls – authorization and the system app picker (FamilyActivityPicker). You never see bundle IDs; you get opaque ApplicationTokens. ManagedSettings – the actual blocking. ManagedSettingsStore().shield.applications = tokens puts a system shield over those apps. Setting it to nil removes it. DeviceActivity – schedules. DeviceActivityCenter.startMonitoring wakes an extension at interval start and end, even when your app is dead. items.summary: I've been using REA to decompile Paste and study how it works. Using that analysis as a reference, I reimplemented the features I use most in a Mac app called Pasto. The project is now open source and free to use, with no subscription. The bottom card panel and interaction patterns take inspiration from Paste. Press ⇧⌘V to browse and search things you've copied, and save frequently used text and links into groups. The repository also contains reverse-engineering notes and implementation comparisons for anyone interested in REA or how clipboard apps work. If you already use Paste, you can import its local groups and their contents into Pasto, keeping their colors and order. Pasto also supports file-based sync through iCloud Drive for clipboard history and groups. It is off by default and can be enabled in Settings → General. Full real-device validation across multiple Macs is still pending. Pasto is written in Swift and supports macOS 14 and later. A single Universal DMG runs on both Intel and Apple silicon Macs. items.title: Boston Dynamics Adds Wheels to Atlas Humanoid
items.summary: Boston Dynamics has equipped its Atlas humanoid with wheels, allowing the robot to rapidly roll across flat terrain while still using its articulated legs to navigate obstacles and uneven surfaces. "The 'experiment' combined classical model-based motor control with whole-body reinforcement learning to maintain dynamic stability across unstructured, real-world terrain," reports The Robot Report. From the report: In addition to learning how to move with wheels for feet, Atlas also performs pirouettes and various aggressive actuation maneuvers. This demonstrates that Atlas can smoothly switch between fast rolling on flat terrain and articulated legged motion over obstacles or irregular surfaces. [Andy Wu, controls engineer for Atlas at Boston Dynamics] trained the system in sim. The system learned all of the behaviors in sim and executed them in real life, with surprising accuracy, according to Wu. Wu said converting Atlas' locomotion style was "wonderfully simple." A single custom adapter mounts an off-the-shelf scooter rim onto Atlas' existing ankle actuator, and that's the only new part in the whole build. items.title: Merging CSV and Excel files without breaking them: encodings, leading zeros, and header drift (.NET notes)
items.summary: "Just concatenate the files" works until the first real-world export shows up. When I was building a small desktop tool in .NET/WPF that merges and splits spreadsheets, three problems caused most of the bugs. Here they are, with the fix I ended up using for each. In practice you'll see at least: UTF-8 UTF-8 with a BOM (common from Excel's "CSV UTF-8" option) GBK / GB18030 (still very common in exports from Chinese finance and e-commerce systems) Open a GBK file as UTF-8 and every Chinese name turns into garbage. A simple detection order that works well: Check for a BOM. If there is one, trust it. Try decoding as strict UTF-8, so invalid bytes throw an error instead of being silently replaced. items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from NBC News: The Food and Drug Administration said Monday that GLP-1 drugmakers must add a warning label about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness. The condition, called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, affects the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain. When blood flow to the nerve is reduced or blocked, it can cause sudden vision loss. The condition is permanent with no known treatment. The FDA said "there is a potential increased risk of rare NAION" in people taking GLP-1 drugs. The agency's requirement applies to all GLP-1s, including Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound, as well as several older GLP-1 diabetes medications. [...] Previous research has found that GLP-1 use may increase the risk of NAION, and Lilly has said it was aware of studies on the potential link. items.title: Day 17: The Connector and the Convergence of Client Responsibilities
items.summary: The previous post, JSON-RPC 2.0: Protocol Choice and the Request Pipeline, was about how a call is handled once it reaches the server. The same contract needs somebody responsible on the client side too: some clients connect to a server on the other side of a network, and some run in the same process as the back end logic, yet both are calling the same method. If everything in between that has nothing to do with the business is left to each front end, there will be as many ways of writing it as there are front ends, and the same mistake will happen once in every one of them. The framework's answer is a Connector layer on the client side as well, which every front end goes through. This post covers: Which things the client has to handle, and why they are collected into one type How a local and a remote connection become the same call, and where the real difference lies Which state belongs to one logged in user, and which belongs to the whole application The layers one save passes through, from the screen to the database, are fixed: Client screen ↓ DataObject: the framework's ViewModel, wrapping a DataSet for the screen to bind to ↓ Connector (this post) ↓ one JSON-RPC call Server AP

items.title: Building Native iOS Apps from Windows with a Team of AI Agents
items.summary: I build OpenV2. Our product is simple to say and hard to ship: you brief a team of AI agents in chat, and they build a native mobile app — SwiftUI for iOS, Kotlin for Android — that you can preview in a simulator and test on a real iPhone. From Windows. No Mac required. This post is about why we built it as a team with roles, not as a single prompt box, and what that workflow looks like in practice. If you want a real iOS app, the traditional path still assumes a Mac, Xcode, and enough SwiftUI experience to not paint yourself into a corner. That is fine if you are a full-time iOS engineer. It is a wall if you are a founder, a PM, or a developer who lives on Windows or Linux and just wants a native app in the store. The other path people try is "prompt an AI and hope." One chat, one model, one giant answer. Sometimes you get something that demos well. Often you get: Generic UI that looks like every other AI-generated screen Architecture that collapses the moment you add auth, payments, or a second platform No clear ownership of research, product decisions, or code quality I wanted something closer to how a small product team actually works: someone owns the brief, someone researches

items.title: Downloaded Is Not Selected: Managing Whisper and Qwen Models in a Native Voice App
items.summary: An “offline AI” switch hides several different questions: is a model present, are its companion files present, and is the runtime actually using it? Treating those as one boolean produces confusing settings and difficult support reports. The local-model catalog in GPT Realtime Assistant makes those distinctions explicit. This article focuses on the inspected download service rather than making a latency claim about every device or language. RealtimeDownloadableModel entries identify a repository, a remote filename, a destination filename, and an installation kind. The catalog includes Whisper Large v3 Turbo variants and Qwen 3 8B variants with different quantizations. That metadata is operational configuration. “Qwen” is not enough information to select a compatible file or explain its storage cost. The precise artifact matters, and companion artifacts can matter too. The status builder resolves the runtime’s chosen Whisper, Qwen, and Qwen-ASR paths separately. For each catalog entry it inspects the local file size and checks that required companion files exist. It reports isInstalled separately from isSelected. items.title: France Accuses Iran of Supermarket Fridge Hacking
items.summary: France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind last month's cyberattacks on fridges and freezers across the country. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions "at the European level." The BBC reports: The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros. Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across several other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked. Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people." He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act." France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond

items.summary: Anthropic has released Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 with "improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision," while cutting Fable's input price and claiming 30% faster responses. TechCrunch reports: It's Anthropic's first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR, which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) -- or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic's AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain. Still, Anthropic's release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. "Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. The move broadens Google's challenge to Nvidia as demand outstrips supply, with Google saying every TPU it currently has is already committed to customers. It pairs with a central processing unit from Advanced Micro Devices and encrypts data at the chip level. The 8i Max is meant for AI applications that need long context windows, meaning the volume of information a model can take into account within one request. Apple announced the rule on September 9, 2026, the same day iOS 27 submissions opened. It applies to every upload, TestFlight builds included, not just App Store releases. The exact day has not been published, and an Apple DTS engineer declined to give one on the developer forums. The researchers suggest this gas is being released from hot magma deep beneath its surface after discovering intriguing new fissures along a massive volcano, indicating the planet may be geologically active after all — or at least it was until relatively recently. The research could have significant implications for the possibility of ancient life on the Red Planet, hinting at a far warmer and thicker atmosphere — and an abundance of liquid water on its surface — in its not-too-distant past.... items.title: iOS Silent Push Notifications That Actually Arrive: content-available, Priority 5 and the Throttling Rules
items.summary: Silent push notifications (Apple calls them background notifications) are the push you send when you don't want to show anything. You just want the app to wake up, fetch new data, refresh a cache or sync a record. They're also the push type developers most often swear "doesn't work." Usually it does work. It just follows rules that visible alerts don't. This guide covers the exact payload and headers, the app-side code, and the reasons a silent push gets delayed or dropped. A silent push is a payload with content-available set to 1 and no alert, sound or badge: { "aps": { "content-available": 1 }, "type": "sync", "since": "2026-11-09T04:00:00Z" } Anything outside aps is your own data and is handed to the app. Keep the total under 4 KB. If you add an alert to the same payload, it's no longer a silent push. It becomes a visible notification that also happens to wake the app, and it follows the visible-alert rules instead. When you call APNs over HTTP/2, a background notification needs these headers: Header Value apns-push-type background apns-priority 5 apns-topic your app's bundle ID Two rules matter here: apns-push-type must be background. items.title: A Mute Button Must Fail Closed: Recording App and Microphone Audio with ReplayKit
items.summary: A screen recording can look correct while sounding completely wrong. A tutorial needs narration above the application’s audio; a demonstration may need only system sound. Treating both inputs as one volume control makes those two jobs unnecessarily difficult. In Reel Screen Recorder, the broadcast extension receives ReplayKit buffers and keeps their source identity until the writer dispatches them. The useful engineering detail is not the slider itself. It is what happens when transforming a buffer fails. The current SampleHandler.handleAudio distinguishes .audioMic from .audioApp and asks the shared settings for recordingGain(forMicrophone:). It then passes the processed buffer, with its original source type, to BroadcastWriter. The writer routes video, app audio, and microphone audio to separate capture functions. Its asset writer uses the MP4 container. This division keeps capture policy out of the file-writing dispatch code and makes it possible to reason about each source independently. items.title: The datacentre arms race hits pause in south-east Asia
items.summary: Power and water constraints are pressuring what seemed like a juggernaut of growth for the region just months ago In early 2026, Thailand’s datacentre industry was on a roll. The country’s board of investment had recently announced approval of datacentre projects from Tiktok, a UAE-based Skyline datacentre and Singapore’s Bridge datacentres, totalling a planned investment of $27bn. As the year has passed, however, what once seemed like a new industrial juggernaut has ground to a halt. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient details for regulation and monitoring. It is not alone in reconsidering datacentre projects. In neighbouring Indonesia, the governor of the country’s most populous province of West Java halted construction on a datacentre due to lack of permits and an incomplete environmental assessment process. items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.
